newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish banks differ on central bank rate prospects.
newsitem.headline: Danish banks differ on central bank rate prospects.

text.p: Two of Denmark's leading banks on Monday disagreed about the prospects of a Danish interest rate cut.
Second-largest Unibank saw a reduction in the National Bank (central bank) discount, CD and repo rates as possible but third-placed BG Bank saw a firmer crown as more likely.

"Growing foreign reserves, relatively low inflation and the stable crown against the mark could lead to consideration of whether the National Bank could reduce the official rates," Unibank Market's weekly money markets newsletter said.
"This could be the National Bank's move instead of buying foreign currency. So far this year its reserves have risen by 23.8 billion crowns, of which 14 billion was in the past two months," it added.
BG Bank took the opposite view.
"If the choice were between cutting rates or letting the crown firm a little we expect the National Bank to allow the crown to get a little stronger, Chief Strategist Thomas Andersen told Reuters.
Analysts at sector-leader Den Danske Bank last week also took the view that a cut was unlikely.
The crown generally stays close to its ERM central rate of 3.8144 to the mark although it has weakened against other currencies, such as the dollar and sterling.
At 1130 GMT it traded at 3.8075 to the mark, 6.5215 to the dollar and 10.6744 against the pound.
The National Bank last acted in August 1996 when it cut the CD and repo rates to 3.50 percent from 3.70 percent, but left the discount and deposit rates unchanged at 3.25 percent.

Bank Governor Bodil Nyboe Andersen last April called for "appreciable" fiscal tightening in 1998 to prevent the economy from overheating and warned that Danish inflation -- 2.1 percent in 1996 by EU calculations -- was higher than that in the country's most important trading partners.
She has repeatedly said that her main priority is keeping the crown stable against the mark.
